what.label: supported
what.says: Akrotiri is a Cycladic Bronze Age settlement on Santorini; its ancient name is unknown and the modern name comes from the nearby village.
quote: is a Cycladic Bronze Age settlement site on the volcanic Greek island of Santorini. The name comes from the nearby village of Akrotiri, the name of the site in antiquity is unknown.

buried.label: supported
buried.says: It was destroyed in the Theran eruption in the 16th century BC and buried in volcanic ash, which preserved its frescoes.
quote: The settlement was destroyed during the Theran eruption sometime in the 16th century BC, and was buried in volcanic ash, which helped preserve its fine frescoes.

canopy.label: supported
canopy.says: The whole site is covered with a giant canopy, so it can be visited even in the hot summer months.
quote: The entire city is covered with a giant canopy, so it can be comfortably visited even during the hot summer months.

pompeii.label: supported
pompeii.says: Like Pompeii, it is remarkably well preserved.
quote: like the Roman ruins of Pompeii after it, it is remarkably well-preserved.

tip.label: supported
tip.says: Only the southern tip of a large town has been uncovered.
quote: Only the southern tip of a large town has been uncovered

village.label: supported
village.says: People lived here as early as the fifth millennium BCE, in a small fishing and farming village.
quote: The earliest evidence for human habitation of Akrotiri can be traced back as early as the fifth millennium BCE when it was a small fishing and farming village.

copper.label: supported
copper.says: Akrotiri sat on the main sailing route between Cyprus and Minoan Crete and became a center for processing copper.
quote: Akrotiri's strategic position on the primary sailing route between Cyprus and Minoan Crete also made it an important point for the copper trade, thus allowing it to become an important centre for processing copper

port.label: supported
port.says: Akrotiri became one of the Aegean's major Bronze Age ports, with objects from Crete, Anatolia, Cyprus, Syria and Egypt.
quote: Akrotiri developed into one of the Aegean's major Bronze Age ports, with recovered objects that came not just from Crete, but also from Anatolia, Cyprus, Syria, and Egypt

minoan.label: supported
minoan.says: Although Cycladic, the site is linked to Minoan civilization through Linear A inscriptions and similar art.
quote: Despite being a Cycladic settlement, the site is associated with the Minoan civilization due to inscriptions in Linear A, and close similarities in artifact and fresco styles.

streets.label: supported
streets.says: Paved streets, an extensive drainage system and fine pottery show the town's sophistication.
quote: paved streets, an extensive drainage system, the production of high-quality pottery and further craft specialization all point to the level of sophistication achieved by the settlement.

walls.label: supported
walls.says: Multi-level buildings, streets and squares survive, with walls standing as high as eight metres; some houses are three storeys high and many stone staircases are intact.
quote: it has revealed complexes of multi-level buildings, streets, and squares with remains of walls standing as high as eight metres
Many of the houses in Akrotiri are major structures, some of them three storeys high.
many stone staircases are still intact

pithoi.label: supported
pithoi.says: The houses contain huge storage jars (pithoi), mills and pottery.
quote: The houses contain huge ceramic storage jars (pithoi), mills, and pottery

water.label: supported
water.says: Pipes with running water and water closets at Akrotiri are the oldest such utilities discovered; twin pipes suggest hot and cold water, probably geothermal.
quote: Pipes with running water and water closets found at Akrotiri are the oldest such utilities discovered.
The pipes run in twin systems, indicating that Therans used both hot and cold water supplies.
The origin of the hot water they circulated in the town probably was geothermal

furniture.label: supported
furniture.says: Ash left hollows where wooden furniture rotted; poured plaster makes casts of beds, tables and chairs.
quote: produced negatives of the disintegrated wooden objects. Using these negatives as molds, liquid plaster-of-Paris can be poured in and produce casts of parts, or even entire pieces of furniture such as beds, tables, chairs or stools.

horns.label: supported
horns.says: In the House of the Benches, 300 to 500 horns were found, painted with ochre; their religious use is unknown.
quote: In the 'House of the Benches' a large deposit of between 300 and 500 horns were found.
painted with patterns in ochre. The religious use is currently unknown.

evacuation.label: supported
evacuation.says: Only a single gold object was found, and no uninterred skeletons, indicating an orderly evacuation.
quote: Only a single gold object has been found, hidden beneath flooring, and no uninterred human skeletal remains have been found. This indicates that an orderly evacuation was performed with little or no loss of life.

took.label: supported
took.says: Because the town was evacuated suddenly, people could take only their most valuable possessions.
quote: its sudden evacuation meant that inhabitants were only able to take their most valuable possessions with them.

warning.label: disputed
warning.says: The volcano gave a few months' warning; earthquakes may have damaged the town months before.
quote: indicate that the volcano gave the local population a few months' warning.
It is also suggested that several months before the eruption, Santorini experienced one or more earthquakes, which damaged the local settlements.

returned.label: disputed
returned.says: Evidence suggests survivors came back to recover possessions and perhaps bury victims.
quote: Evidence at the site suggests that survivors returned and attempted to recover their possessions and perhaps to bury victims.

date.label: disputed
date.says: The exact year is not known; radiocarbon places it most probably between 1620 and 1530 BC.
quote: There is a variety of dating evidence for the eruption, but its exact year is not known. Radiocarbon dating places it most probably between 1620 and 1530 BC

frescoes-why.label: supported
frescoes-why.says: Akrotiri's frescoes are much better preserved than those from Knossos and other sites on Crete.
quote: they are much better preserved than those that were already known from Knossos and other sites on Crete

colors.label: supported
colors.says: Theran painters used white, yellow, red, brown, blue and black, apparently from minerals.
quote: The colors used in Theran painting include white, yellow, red, brown, blue and black.
look as though they are mineral based

monkeys.label: supported
monkeys.says: In 1969 the Blue Monkeys fresco was found in Room Beta 6; the rocks the monkeys climb look like the volcanic rocks near the site.
quote: In 1969, the fresco of the Blue Monkeys in Room Beta 6 was discovered
The rocky landscape which the monkeys are depicted climbing upon mimics the similar volcanic rocks near the site presently.

spring.label: supported
spring.says: In 1970 the Spring Fresco was found in Room Delta 2, the first fresco found perfectly preserved and still standing where it was installed.
quote: In 1970 the Spring Fresco was uncovered in Room Delta 2. It is the first fresco to have been found perfectly preserved and still standing in its original installed position.

scenes.label: supported
scenes.says: More complete frescoes show antelopes, a man holding fish, a flotilla of boats with dolphins; others show saffron-gatherers offering crocus to a seated woman, perhaps a goddess.
quote: two antelopes painted with a confident calligraphic line, a man holding fish strung by their gills, a flotilla of pleasure boats that are accompanied by leaping dolphins
depict "saffron-gatherers" offering crocus-stamens to a seated woman, perhaps a goddess important to the Akrotiri culture.

boxers.label: supported
boxers.says: The Boxer Fresco shows two young boys wearing boxing gloves; it was found in room B1 of Building Beta with the Antelope Fresco.
quote: It is a fresco depicting two young boys wearing boxing gloves and belts
This particular fresco was found in room B1 of Building Beta along with the Antelope Fresco.

boxers-unknown.label: disputed
boxers-unknown.says: It is impossible to know whether the match was a competition or routine sport.
quote: It is impossible to know whether the match was a competitive one or simply a routine sport.

museum.label: supported
museum.says: Excavated finds are shown in the Museum of Prehistoric Thera, away from the site.
quote: Excavated artifacts have been installed in a museum distant from the site (Museum of Prehistoric Thera), with many objects and artworks presented.

fouque.label: supported
fouque.says: The earliest excavations on the island were by French geologist F. Fouque in 1867.
quote: The earliest excavations on the island of Santorini were conducted by French geologist F. Fouque in 1867 after some local people found old artifacts at a quarry.

marinatos-1967.label: supported
marinatos-1967.says: The extensive modern excavation was started in 1967 by Spyridon Marinatos.
quote: The extensive modern excavation was started in 1967 by Spyridon Marinatos

theory.label: supported
theory.says: Marinatos had argued that Thera's eruption destroyed Neopalatial Crete, and decided to dig on Thera to test it.
quote: In the same year, Marinatos published an article in the journal Antiquity arguing that the Neopalatial civilisation of Crete had been destroyed by the eruption of the volcanic island of Thera
Marinatos decided to excavate on Thera to test his hypothesis

theory-rejected.label: disputed
theory-rejected.says: Later analysis showed the eruption came several generations before the end of Neopalatial civilization, now generally attributed to human causes.
quote: more detailed analysis of the pottery from Crete and Akrotiri indicated that the eruption occurred several generations before the end of Neopalatial civilisation, which is now generally attributed to human causes.

tunnel.label: supported
tunnel.says: The remains were buried under about 150 feet of pumice; Marinatos tunnelled in from a gully.
quote: which were buried beneath approximately 150 feet (46 metres) of pumice, by tunnelling into the site from a gully that cut through it.

five-days.label: supported
five-days.says: Within five days of the start on 24 May, he found Minoan-style remains; forty local pumice miners supported the dig.
quote: Within five days of the excavation's start on 24 May, Marinatos uncovered remains of a structure in the Minoan architectural style
The excavation was supported by forty local pumice miners

death.label: disputed
death.says: Marinatos died while excavating at Akrotiri on 1 October 1974; contemporary accounts said a fall, a later story a collapsing wall.
quote: On 1 October 1974, Marinatos died while excavating at Akrotiri. Contemporary accounts related that he had died from a fall, while giving instructions to a worker; a later narrative emerged that he had been struck by a collapsing wall.

grave.label: supported
grave.says: He was first buried on the site near where he died; his grave was later moved outside the ruins.
quote: He was initially buried on the excavation site, near the place of his death; his grave was subsequently moved outside the ruins.

junta.label: supported
junta.says: He was an enthusiastic supporter of Greece's military junta, and his leadership was criticised for cronyism.
quote: He was an enthusiastic supporter of the junta
His leadership of the Archaeological Service has been criticised for its cronyism

doumas.label: supported
doumas.says: After Marinatos's death, Christos Doumas took over the excavations.
quote: after Marinatos' death, Christos Doumas took over as the head of excavations.

collapse.label: supported
collapse.says: In 2005 a new protective roof collapsed just before completion, killing one visitor; the site was closed until April 2012.
quote: In 2005, a new roof structure, meant to protect the site, collapsed just before its completion, killing one visitor.
Between 2005 and April 2012, the site was closed to visitors.

goat.label: supported
goat.says: In 2018 a small shrine with a marble figurine of a woman was found in the House of the Thrania, near Xeste 3, where a golden goat was found in 1999.
quote: In October 2018, a small shrine with a marble figurine of a woman was discovered in the "House of the Thrania" which is located near Xeste 3, where a golden goat was found in 1999.

atlantis.label: disputed
atlantis.says: Marinatos suggested the eruption lies behind Plato's Atlantis; current scholarship does not support this.
quote: Spyridon Marinatos, the discoverer of the Akrotiri archaeological site, suggested that the Minoan eruption is reflected in Plato's story of Atlantis.
However, this view is not supported by current scholarship.

parts.name: Arrival
parts.stand: Just inside the covered site, at the first point where you can look down over the buried streets.

paras.t: Welcome to Akrotiri, a Bronze Age town buried in volcanic ash in the 1500s BC. Like Pompeii, it's remarkably well preserved.
Here's something to start with: nobody knows what its people called it. Akrotiri is just the name of the modern village nearby.

The huge roof over your head covers the whole site, which is why you can visit even in the summer heat. And what you see is only the southern tip of a much larger town. The rest is still under the ground around you.
Watch your step on the walkways and any stairs, and take your time.

parts.name: A town that traded
parts.stand: Move along the walkway until you can see down into a street lined with walls.

paras.t: This was a busy port. It sat on the main sailing route between Cyprus and Minoan Crete, and it became a center for working copper.

It started small. People lived here as early as the fifth millennium BC, in a fishing and farming village. Over time it grew into one of the major Bronze Age ports of the Aegean. Objects found here came from Crete, from Anatolia, Cyprus, Syria and Egypt.
Strictly, this was a Cycladic town, not a Cretan one. But its writing, Linear A, and the style of its art tie it closely to the Minoan civilization of Crete.

parts.name: Walking the streets
parts.stand: Stay where you can see down into the streets and the house walls.

paras.t: Look down at the houses. Some stood three stories high, and walls here still stand as tall as eight meters. Many of the stone staircases are still intact.

This was a sophisticated place: paved streets and an extensive drainage system. And here's the remarkable bit. Pipes with running water and water closets found at Akrotiri are the oldest such utilities ever discovered. The pipes run in pairs, which suggests both hot and cold water. The hot water probably came from the volcano itself.

Inside the houses, the excavators found huge storage jars, called pithoi, along with mills and pottery. Where wooden furniture rotted away inside the ash, it left a hollow, a perfect mold. Pour in liquid plaster, and out comes a cast of a bed, a table or a stool.
Some things remain a mystery. In one building, the House of the Benches, they found between 300 and 500 animal horns, painted with ochre patterns. What they were used for in worship, nobody knows.

parts.name: Where did everyone go?
parts.stand: Pause anywhere along the walkway with a view down into the houses.

paras.t: Now the question everyone asks. Where are the people? Unlike Pompeii, no skeletons lie in these streets, and only a single gold object has been found. It looks like the town was evacuated in an orderly way.

Scholars think the volcano gave a few months' warning. Earthquakes may have damaged the town first. People left in a hurry, carrying only their most valuable things, and that's why so much pottery stayed behind.
There's even evidence that survivors came back afterward, to recover their belongings and perhaps to bury their dead. What happened to them after that, nobody knows.
And when did it happen? The exact year isn't known. Radiocarbon dating places it most probably between 1620 and 1530 BC.

parts.name: The painted walls
parts.stand: Stand where you have a good view of the larger houses.

paras.t: The ash also saved its wall paintings, far better preserved than those from Knossos on Crete. Many finds are now in the Museum of Prehistoric Thera, in Fira.
Their scenes are full of life: two antelopes, a man holding a catch of fish, a flotilla of boats with leaping dolphins, and girls gathering saffron for a seated woman, perhaps a goddess.

The painters worked in white, yellow, red, brown, blue and black, colors that seem to come from minerals. In 1969, the Blue Monkeys were found in a room the excavators called Beta 6. The rocks the monkeys are climbing look just like the volcanic rocks around this site. In 1970, the Spring Fresco turned up in Room Delta 2, the first fresco here found perfectly preserved and still standing where it was painted.
There's also a fresco of two young boys wearing boxing gloves, found in Building Beta. Was it a real match, or just practice? Nobody knows.
The great excavation here was begun in 1967 by the Greek archaeologist Spyridon Marinatos.
He wasn't the first to dig on the island. The French geologist Fouque dug on Santorini in 1867, after local people found old objects in a quarry.
He came with a theory: that this eruption had destroyed the Minoan palace civilization on Crete. He wanted to test it. The town lay under about 150 feet of pumice, so he tunnelled in from a gully.
Within five days of starting on 24 May, he hit walls in the Minoan style, with forty local pumice miners helping him dig.

History has been mixed on his theory. Scholars now think the eruption came several generations before the end of Minoan palace society on Crete. And his other famous idea, that the eruption lies behind Plato's Atlantis, isn't supported by current scholarship either.
He was a complicated man, too. He was an enthusiastic supporter of Greece's military junta, and his leadership of the Archaeological Service was criticized for cronyism.
In 1974, Marinatos died here, while excavating. Nobody's sure how: reports at the time said he fell, and a later story said a wall collapsed on him. Christos Doumas took over the dig.
He was first buried on the site, near where he died. His grave was later moved outside the ruins.

Work has not always been easy. In 2005 a new protective roof collapsed just before it was finished, killing one visitor, and the site stayed closed until April 2012. But the finds keep coming: a golden goat in 1999, and in 2018 a small shrine with a marble figurine of a woman.

parts.name: Closing
parts.stand: Take one last look down over the streets before you leave.

paras.t: Picture the last morning here. People closing their doors, choosing what to carry, leaving the rest behind. Walking these streets, it feels as if they just stepped out for a moment.
